messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 52-year-old European American film director, has been struggling to cope with the aftermath of a life-threatening car accident he experienced six months ago. The event left an indelible mark on his psyche, transforming his daily life and professional endeavors in profound ways. On the night of the accident, John was returning home from a film festival when a drunk driver swerved into his lane, causing a violent collision that sent his car spinning out of control. Miraculously, he survived with only minor injuries, but the psychological trauma lingered. The images of that dark night and the deafening sounds of shattering glass and screeching tires continue to haunt him. Since then, John has found himself avoiding situations that remind him of the event. For example, he no longer drives at night because being in darkness brings back the terrifying memories so vividly. This avoidance extends to his professional life as well; he often hesitates when filming scenes with nighttime settings or involving loud noises, fearing they might trigger flashbacks. John’s thoughts are constantly occupied by questions about why this happened to him and how it has changed him fundamentally. He struggles to articulate the event in words but finds himself consumed by vivid visual memories that replay endlessly in his mind. The clarity of these memories intensifies his feelings of inadequacy and self-doubt, further eroding his sense of identity. These negative appraisals—feeling inadequate, believing he is a poor coper, and recognizing the unrecognizable person he has become—are at the core of John’s suffering. They drive him to adopt maladaptive strategies such as seeking distraction through work or other activities to avoid confronting his memories directly. However, these avoidance tactics often lead him into new triggers that exacerbate his symptoms. For instance, John was once startled by a sudden loud noise on set while filming an action sequence. The sound triggered intense hypervigilance and panic, leaving him shaken and unable to focus for the rest of the day. This incident reinforced his negative beliefs about himself, making him feel even more inadequate and convinced that he is not capable of handling such stress. John’s heightened sense of threat manifests in various ways. He becomes superalert in environments with unexpected sounds or loud noises, believing that these could be precursors to another traumatic event. This hypervigilance has affected his personal relationships as well; his partner often notices him being overly cautious and anxious during conversations, especially if the environment is noisy. The cycle of negative appraisals, memory intrusions, threat perception, and maladaptive strategies continues to tighten its grip on John’s life. His attempts to distract himself or avoid triggering situations only serve to reinforce his feelings of inadequacy and fear. He has come to believe that he will never be able to return to the person he was before the accident. What finally brought John to seek help is the realization that these coping mechanisms are not sustainable. He is most afraid of losing control completely, both professionally and personally, but at the same time, he hopes for a way to regain his confidence and normalcy. Seeking therapy feels like a last-ditch effort to break free from this vicious cycle before it consumes him entirely. In conclusion, John’s journey after the accident has been one marked by avoidance, hypervigilance, and relentless negative appraisals, all driven by vivid and nonverbal memories of that fateful night. The tight interplay between these components has left him feeling trapped in a loop he cannot break alone.
